lena.name: Dr. Lena Reyes
lena.role: field biologist (a scientist who studies animals in the wild)

case.title: The Refuge Sign
case.hook: Good news! The refuge read our case report on the spoonbill. Now they want a sign about it for the boardwalk where I found the soggy notebook. Three people sent drafts, and I taped them into my notebook. Only one can go on the sign.
case.question: Which draft explains how the spoonbill survives, and what would make the other two better?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

stills.alt: A photo of a spoonbill feeding, with three labels: beak, legs, feathers. There are no arrows and no sentences.
A beautiful old painting of a pink spoonbill bending down to the water. There are no labels, arrows or words about the bird.
The spoonbill photo with labels, arrows from the beak and legs to what they do, and a caption about food.
Pink spoonbills standing in a shallow lagoon, with mangroves behind them.

case.stillsCredit: Drafts A and C are built on a real photo: roseate spoonbill feeding, Andy Morffew (CC BY 2.0). Draft B: Roseate Spoonbill, Robert Havell after John James Audubon, 1836, National Gallery of Art (CC0). Lagoon: James St. John (CC BY 2.0). All via Wikimedia Commons.

clues.t: A label only names a part. An arrow from the part to what it acts on, with a few action words, turns a drawing into a model.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: upgrade the drawing
clues.t: A strong model has three things: labels, arrows that show action, and a caption that ties the part to a survival need.
Every model follows the same chain: structure → action → survival need. A color or a name alone isn’t a link.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: the model kit
clues.t: You built a model on a real photo. Any picture, even a pretty one, becomes a model when you add labels, arrows and a caption.

solve.title: Which draft goes on the sign?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Draft B, the painting, because it’s the most beautiful.
options.why: Check Clue 4. A painting is lovely, but with no labels or arrows a visitor can’t tell what the beak does.

options.t: Draft A, because it names every part.
options.why: Check Clue 1. Names alone don’t tell what the parts do.

options.t: Draft C. It has labels, arrows that show what the beak and legs do, and a caption about food. Draft A needs arrows and a caption. Draft B needs labels, arrows and a caption.
options.why: Case closed for good! Draft C is a model: it explains, not just names. Now write your case report: it’s the questions below.

arrow.title: Point the arrow
todo: Drag the arrow to what the teeth act on, or tap that box.
Pick the action words for your arrow.

why.q: What does an arrow do in a model?
why.t: In a model, an arrow points from a part to the thing it acts on. The words on the arrow tell what the part does.

arrow.alt: A close-up of an American alligator’s head resting on the ground, with its teeth showing along its jaw.
arrow.credit: American alligator head, Stephenx77, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).
arrow.q1: Step 1: Where should the arrow point?

targets.miss: Teeth don’t do anything to the sun. What do they grab?
A gator doesn’t eat rocks. What does it catch with its teeth?

arrow.q2: Step 2: What do the teeth do? Pick the words for your arrow.

actions.miss: That’s a feeling, not a job. What do the teeth do to the fish?
That’s just the label again. What do the teeth DO?

arrow.win: That’s a tiny model! Drawing 2 tells a friend what the teeth do, not just what they’re called. That’s a clue.

upgrade.afterText: Each kind is good for a different job
upgrade.title: Upgrade the drawing
todo: Answer each step to add one thing to the photo.
Watch the meter at the top.

why.t: A labeled drawing names a part. Each thing you add tells the reader more about how the part helps the bird survive.

upgrade.alt: A pink roseate spoonbill bending down with its long beak in dark, shallow water.
upgrade.credit: Roseate spoonbill feeding, Andy Morffew, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0).

steps.q: Add a label. Which part will this model explain?

opts.miss: Pink is a color, not a part.
That’s the whole bird. A label names one part.

steps.q: Add an arrow. What does the beak do?

opts.miss: That describes its shape. What does it DO?
That’s its shape again. What job does it do in the water?

steps.q: Add a caption that ties it to a survival need.

opts.t: This beak helps the spoonbill meet its survival need for food.

opts.miss: That’s just a name. Which survival need does the beak help with?
Pretty isn’t a survival need. Food, water, air, shelter or safety?

upgrade.win: Label, arrow, caption: that’s a model! That’s a clue.

chain.title: Chain it
todo: Drag each card into its link, or tap a card and then a link.

why.t: A model explains in order: first the part, then what it does, then which survival need it meets.

chain.hint: Drag each card into its link, or tap a card and then a link. Two cards don’t belong in the chain.
chain.missX: That card is true, or it’s a name, but it isn’t a link. A link is a part, what the part does, or the need it meets.

missSlot.s: That card is a part. Put it in the Structure link.
missSlot.a: That card is an action, something a part does.
missSlot.n: That card is a survival need: food, water, air, shelter or safety.

orgs.name: Green tree frog
orgs.why: Green skin → blends in → safety. That’s camouflage, a color adaptation.

orgs.name: Gopher tortoise

cards.t: Dig a long burrow in the sand

orgs.why: Shovel legs → dig a burrow → shelter. Hundreds of other Florida animals use those burrows too.

orgs.name: Anhinga

cards.t: Long, pointed beak on an S-shaped neck

orgs.why: Pointed beak → spears fish → food. The anhinga model in Part 2 shows the same chain.

orgs.name: Longleaf pine

cards.t: Keeps the heat of a fire away from the living wood

orgs.why: Thick bark → blocks heat → safety from fire. Plants have structures that help them survive, too.

chain.win: Four chains built! Every strong model follows this chain. That’s a clue.

q1.A: Colors don’t explain anything. What shows how the parts work?
q1.B: Size doesn’t make a model stronger. What do arrows and captions add?

q2.A: A survival need is something it must have, like food. Is green skin a need, or something that helps it?
q2.C: Skin color is on the outside of the frog, not inside.

q3.B: Computer models count. But are they the only kind?
q3.C: A fancy drawing isn’t needed. What makes any model count?

ans-2: Think about Drawing 1 and Drawing 2 in the Warm-Up.
A label names a part. What does a model add? Annotate means to add labels, arrows and short notes.
Try: A labeled drawing only ___. A model ___. When you annotate, you ___.
ans-3: A fluke is a manatee’s wide, flat tail. It pushes the water so the manatee can swim.
A flat drawing can’t bend or move. What could you see if you could turn a 3-D model in your hands?
Try: A 3-D model shows how the fluke ___. Its function is to ___.

welcome.label: Welcome · the refuge sign
welcome.script: Good news from the refuge! They read our case report about the spoonbill, and now they want a sign for the boardwalk where I found that soggy notebook. Three people sent drafts. One is a photo with labels. One is a beautiful old painting. One is a photo with arrows. Only one can go on the sign. Help me decide which one really explains how the spoonbill survives.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · point the arrow (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Here’s a trick I use in my field notebook. When I draw an animal, I don’t just write names next to the parts. I draw an arrow from the part to whatever it acts on. One arrow can turn a drawing into an explanation. Try it with this alligator’s teeth.

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Say each word; for annotate, add an arrow and a note to a quick sketch on a whiteboard.

part2.label: Part 2 · upgrade the drawing (Clue 2)
part2.script: Let’s upgrade a drawing, one step at a time. First a label, then an arrow, then a caption. Watch the meter at the top. It shows how close your drawing is to being a real model.

part3.label: Part 3 · chain it (Clue 3)
part3.script: Every model I make follows the same chain. First the part. Then what the part does. Then which survival need it meets. Build a chain for four Florida organisms. Watch out: two cards in each set don’t belong in the chain.

explore.label: Part 4 · the model kit (Clue 4)
explore.script: Now it’s your turn to be the scientist. Pick an organism, tap a part on the real photo, and point its arrow. Then choose what the part does and which need it meets. When you finish, you’ll have a real model, just like the ones in my notebook.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: You’ve got all four clues. Crack the case at the top of this tab: which draft should go on the refuge sign? Then build your own model in Part C. Your answers save as you type.

partc.label: Part C · build an annotated model

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: Someone once told me that drawings aren’t real science. I laughed, because my notebook is full of them! What do you think? Pick your side, choose two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.notes: Celebrate; tease week 12 (senses, brain and the four trail cameras).
closing.script: Case closed for good! Draft C goes on the sign, and visitors will learn how the spoonbill finds its food. Next week, we’ll find out what happens inside an animal when it notices something: its senses, its brain, and what it does next.

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how a model shows what a part does?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: A model uses arrows and a caption to explain what a part does.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “model”, “arrows”, “caption” and “explain”. Those words carry the idea. Small words like “a” and “to” don’t.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
